utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This afternoon, we will hear the opening statement of the Defence first. If we have time, we will call the first witness. As for the break, I'm entirely in the hands of the parties. If you feel that you need a break, just inform us. Mr. Morrissey, are you in a position to deliver your opening statement, I mean physical condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the question, Your Honour, but yes, the time has come to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Your Honours. It's time to start the Defence case and yet paradoxically it's almost finished already because it was the Defence position to put as much evidence as was possible to put through the Prosecution case. It was the Defence position to elicit answers from the witnesses as the Prosecution themselves did which is relevant to the indictment that's before you, not to any other case, not to any other document, but to that indictment. For that reason, the Defence asked many questions of witnesses and put many documents to those witnesses, and therefore, Your Honours, the Defence case is going to be now - what remains of it - is going to be short and focused on some specific issues. The reason why the Defence took the stance that we did is because of a fundamental feature of this Tribunal, and that is that the onus or the burden of proof is squarely upon the Prosecution in this case to prove the guilt of Sefer Halilovic beyond a reasonable doubt as charged in the indictment that you have. And in light of that, it's for the Prosecution to exclude every other reasonable conclusion than that of guilt of Sefer Halilovic. Now, this Tribunal consists of professional judges who have been in the position of having to apply this standard before and it's not intended in any way to be a bad reflection upon the Tribunal to make some comments about what exactly it means to be presumed innocent. In the case of Sefer Halilovic, it is anything but an artificial presumption. What I'd like to do is just to read a quote to you from the Pohl case, an old case, that says this: "Every defendant in a criminal case is presumed to be innocent until the Prosecution, by competent and credible proof, has shown his guilt to the exclusion of every reasonable doubt. This presumption of innocence follows him throughout the trial until such degree of proof has been adduced. Beyond a reasonable doubt does not mean beyond a vain, imaginary or fanciful doubt, but means that the defendant's guilt must be fully proved to a moral certainty before he's condemned. And the human significance of that approach is apparent when you deal with an accused person like Sefer Halilovic. Of course, that protection attaches to everyone in this Tribunal but in the case of Halilovic, you know because the Prosecution have led the evidence to this effect, that he was not an ethnic cleanser. He was not a person who was for division, who favoured cruelty or anarchy. He was a person who took over the management of the Bosnian army when it was in its infancy and throughout one and a half trying years of involvement in that army, he did nothing but endeavour to bring order to that army. The Prosecution evidence clearly proved that Halilovic was a person who attempted to bring order, and in a situation of potential chaos and collapse of a state, the effort to bring order is itself a significant contribution to human rights, and a background against which other human rights can be developed. And a background against which the human rights required by international humanitarian law to be protected can be protected. And as well as attempting to bring order, Sefer Halilovic attempted to promote a vision of the army and of the state which was of a multi-ethnic Bosnia. You are absolutely not called upon here to adjudicate the rights and wrongs of the struggle between the warring parties, and you do not have to and there is law to say that you shouldn't. But you can take very strongly into account the stance that Sefer Halilovic always adopted, and that was to stand against the division of Bosnia along ethnic lines and the division of the army along ethnic lines. Always Sefer Halilovic stood for an army which would be multi-ethnic in character, based upon the Presidency platform which was put into evidence through General Karavelic, who was one of the last witnesses. And in those circumstances, it takes a huge amount of believing that Sefer Halilovic could commit the crimes he's charged with. It's an amazing story that a person such as Halilovic could commit these crimes. So the evidence against him needs to be very clear, very unequivocal, and it's for that reason that I take the trouble and I trouble you to hear what you already know, and that is that he's presumed innocent and that the Prosecution have a very high mountain to climb and a very high hurdle to jump before they can satisfy you that he is guilty of the crime he's charged with, and it has to be remembered as well that that crime is murder. There was a moment of tragedy in this Court when Sefer Halilovic sat in the dock and Ramiz Delalic, Celo, gave evidence. And we ask the Tribunal to consider whether that is bringing peace and stability to Bosnia. To put the peace maker in the dock, and a man who the Prosecution in their own pleadings, and I make it quite clear when I say this, I rely on the indictment, the Prosecution position was and presumably remains that Ramiz Delalic himself was a war criminal who was a commander of units of the 9th Brigade detached from that unit, and who gave an order to bury bodies. I'll say something more about this later but, of course, you would wonder and you would have wondered at the time, why do they call Ramiz Delalic? The answer is because they had to. He has been in their case since 1998. He's there today. Never can they escape him. They are tied to Ramiz Delalic, and there they will stay. Your Honours, could I move from that to some applications of the burden and the standard of proof in this Tribunal? The Prosecution have to prove, and it's axiomatic that they do, each element of the crime beyond reasonable doubt. And that applies of course to each of the three paths which the Prosecution seek to follow to a conviction for murder in this Tribunal. They must prove each of the elements beyond a reasonable doubt and a failure on any of those elements results in acquittal. The same standard of proof applies to important or significant facts in the case. Now, it is never the case that the Prosecutor must prove every detail beyond a reasonable doubt. Always, the Prosecutor will lead evidence that will change in some small particulars, the memory of witnesses changes, but any fact that is significant in the Prosecution case, that is a necessary step on the way to a conviction, must itself be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Let me give an example of what I mean. It's important when the Prosecution accuse Sefer Halilovic of failing to prevent the crimes at Grabovica, it's important in the Prosecution case to say that he was at the village of Grabovica on the afternoon of the 8th of September. I'll just interpose something there. Even that part of their case is new. It's a new part of their case and it's changed since the indictment. But I'm going to take you to the indictment. At the moment I wish to illustrate the standard of proof and burden of proof issue. Now, the Prosecution say that Mr. Halilovic was there on that afternoon and as a result of being there he was in a position to overhear a bizarre comment by the inspection team member Vehbija Karic. And according to one view of Prosecution evidence, to observe the response or the discussions that were going on at that time. Now, the Defence, of course, contest that Karic ever said any such thing and that's another dispute for another time, but at the moment we are dealing with the question, was Halilovic there? And in that regard, the Prosecutor called evidence from two witnesses, Witness D, of course, and another witness, named Muhanic [phoen] and their stories were quite different from each other. And you'll recall that one said that there was a lineup under a balcony where a lonesome Croatian person was standing and that when Karic said what he said, it was unlikely that Halilovic was in a position to hear that. But Witness D said something different. He said it was outside another house and that the comment was made and that Halilovic heard it. Was Sefer Halilovic there? Well, against that proposition you have the evidence of other witnesses, and in the closing speech we are going to go through all of them, of course, but now I'll just point to Namik Dzankovic. So, Namik Dzankovic was a witness called by the Prosecutor, unchallenged, no attempt made by the Prosecution to impeach him, you would think a sensible, viable witness, no particular purpose to serve in saying that Halilovic wasn't there, and he said Sefer Halilovic wasn't there. So did the Prosecution prove beyond reasonable doubt that Halilovic was there? The Defence would say no. I'd say when you have a dispute between witnesses of course you as professional judges can assess those witnesses. But in the absence of a compelling reason to accept Witness D, you would not find that fact to be proved. And Witness D was not a compelling witness. He was a blinding disaster. Witness D changed his story, had a purpose to serve, is an associate of Ramiz Delalic and, in my submission, would not be believed even if he was not contradicted by other witnesses. In other words if he stood alone, he would still not get you beyond that standard because he is so unreliable. But of course, he is contradicted. There is an example of a key fact to which that standard of proof must be applied. The next general point we want to make is this. We ask the Tribunal to recall the importance of certainty and stability in the law. We suspect that the Prosecution will argue for some novel interpretations and extensions of international humanitarian law and we expect that it will be said that a failure to do that might result in gaps or unfortunate lacunae in the protections offered to civilians. While this is a mature body of law now and this Tribunal is a mature body, you are -- you may apply the law and we ask you to be cautious, conservative, and mainstream. We do not ask for exceptions to be created out of the law to protect Sefer Halilovic. And the Defence intends to put in its legal submissions at the end of the case what we hope is a very mainstream case in terms of the law and how it applies. Nor do we think that the Halilovic case would create any precedents if mainstream law were applied, because the circumstances of this case are really very unusual. And the situation that Mr. Halilovic was in of attempting to bring order to an army and himself being the -- one of the guiding spirits behind the rules of procedure for the military security service, the military body which had the competence to look into these affairs once they happened, it will be our submission at the end that you will be able to accommodate fully an acquittal and a comfortable acquittal for Sefer Halilovic without in any way diminishing the protection that international law offers to victims. And without diminishing the effectiveness of this Tribunal in the work it does in the broader community. And what we ask fundamentally and as an application of that is that the Court sticks to the indictment, that you stay with the Prosecution's indictment. Above all, we ask that the Court hold the Prosecutor to what they pleaded in this indictment. Now, the Defence means no personal attack on the Prosecution, and although there have been some warm moments in the Tribunal and in this particular courtroom, what we say is a comment about the Prosecution as a body, and not aimed at individuals in the least. The Defence admires the Prosecution's approach and their tenacity and the ingenuity with which they have sought to find a way to convict Mr. Halilovic and to reconstruct out of the ashes of the original case something new. But it can't be allowed. You can admire the intellectual effort but you can't have the rule of law and that sort of change. We are going to go through the indictment and we are going to look to see what they sought to prove and whether they did, and the reason we do that now is because that was the Defence case. It happened during the Prosecution case. Before I commence on that I wanted to say this. The evidence that the Defence is proposing to lead here is narrow and focused. It chiefly relates to the investigation of the Uzdol killings. There will be some evidence relevant to the mode of investigation that is open to military security services in Bosnia, and in that regard the witness who the Prosecution renounced calling Bahrudin Comor is going to be called to give some evidence about that, if not six weeks ago, then now in court. Otherwise, the focus chiefly is on the issue of Uzdol because there are gaps. The Prosecution conducted a case there that was minimal and too minimal, and the Defence has decided to meet certain of the gaps in relation to that. But with regard to the failure to prevent the crime at Grabovica, there is little or no evidence that's going to be called about that. We will rely on the evidence that has been led, and likewise there is little evidence, though some, to be led in respect to the failure to punish, the Prosecution alleges. Your Honours, I turn now to the crime of murder that Sefer Halilovic is charged with. There are three bases of liability as the Court knows. One is to failing to prevent the crime at Grabovica. The second is failing to punish the crime at Grabovica, the third is failing to punish a different set of killings at Uzdol. Each path independently leads to conviction of the crime of murder and therefore the Prosecution says that it's appropriate to proceed with all three under the one indictment. It is not the time to put an argument about that. The time period for challenging the indictment passed without it being challenged for reasons which do not need to concern the Court now. It is apparent and must have been apparent as the trial unfolded that there were difficulties with charging three such incidents. Or three such episodes of criminality under one indictment. But, however, it is not the time now to deal with that and we are not going to. So I want to deal first of all with the crime that's alleged of murder by means of failing to prevent a crime at Grabovica. Now, Your Honours, if you like, the big intuitive picture much that which is not meant to be a pleading but is meant to be simply a description of what happened there from the Defence point of view is quite plain. The Defence says that Sefer Halilovic is not guilty of that crime. He did not fail culpably to prevent the killings at Grabovica. The Defence says the Prosecution did not establish - did not establish - that Sefer Halilovic was in effective control of the killers. A preliminary comment is the Prosecution did not prove who the killers were in the main but identified two such people. But however, that's particulars which we will come to a bit later on. Secondly the Prosecution said -- sorry, the Defence says that the Prosecution did not prove that Sefer Halilovic had the relevant kind of notice pursuant to Article 7(3). Your Honours, the Prosecution in the indictment clearly and unambiguously pleaded a case of actual notice. They did not prove that case. It's evident from the evidence that the Prosecution led that they wish to proceed to attempt to prove a case of constructive notice against Sefer Halilovic. We say they shouldn't be permitted to do that but if they are, they did not succeed in proving it, nor did they come close to proving it. And it's for that reason that I mentioned at the start of this opening address that it's important to bear in mind Sefer Halilovic's character as shown in the evidence. He stood for a multi-ethnic army and a multi-ethnic Bosnia. There was an attempt made in the opening speech of the Prosecutor to suggest that he was an angry or bitter man. That's not pleaded. But that suggestion was made, but it has to be borne steadily in mind that whether you take the idealistic view of Sefer Halilovic as someone who favoured a multi-ethnic army and community, or whether you take the view that he was self-serving even to a small degree, the fact is no one suggested he departed from that position. If he was seeking power in the unspecified way the Prosecution has hinted, his position was that he disputed with Izetbegovic the direction that was being taken and he always appeared to stand for that multiethnic character of the army and of the community and therefore, these crimes were absolutely against his interest, whether you view him as good or self-serving, these crimes did not serve his interest. In fact they were radically damaging to it and must have been seen in that light at all times. So the Defence says that generally speaking what the evidence discloses, and this is a global view of the evidence, is that Sefer Halilovic was a person who after his removal as the head of the army was unlikely to be given any command or authority. He was under surveillance measures, his phone was being tapped. When he went down to Herzegovina, it was pursuant to an order which you have in evidence, the order of the 30th of the 8th, which on its face does not give him command of any particular units for any particular operation, but gives in point 3 of the order a very limited power. The Defence says the evidence showed that Halilovic as Chief of Staff had no independent place in the chain of command, but that he was empowered to give certain orders if authorised to by his commander, as chiefs of staff are. The Defence says it was never proved that he was the commander of an operation, that there was no de jure case established, no appointment of Halilovic, no operations group. The Defence says that the Prosecution did not prove that Sefer Halilovic, whether commander or not, had effective control over the troops or others who committed the atrocities, those which can be proved, at Grabovica. The Defence says in that regard that it was never proved that Sefer Halilovic had de facto authority or control over those troops at the relevant time. It must be proved that Sefer Halilovic had effective control and such control has to be clearly distinguished from influence. The Prosecution mounted an unpleaded case during evidence of influence, but influence does not equate to effective control. The Defence takes issue that the Prosecution proved influence to any significant degree, but to the extent that such evidence was led, it did not establish effective control. You might take the view of the evidence there that those troops at Grabovica, the ones who did the killing, were thoroughly out of control, that the command arrangements were non-existent, and that the Prosecution simply did not prove how the chain of command operated, what the role of company commanders were, the role of Zulfikar Alispago, the role of Ramiz Delalic or any other real or imaginary commanders interposed in between, including Senad Pecar, Zuti, Malco Rovcanin, or other candidates designed to shield Ramiz Delalic from indictment. Now the Defence said that the evidence disclosed that the troops were billeted at the village pursuant to a decision that was not criminally negligent but which had nothing to do with Sefer Halilovic. The deposition evidence of Vehbija Karic made it quite clear how that was done, and Karic had no purpose to serve of his own to take on his own shoulders, as he did in that deposition, the decision. But the reason for taking that decision emerged from the evidence with a number of facts that were important ones. Most of the soldiers in the 9th Brigade were considered to be decent people. The weight of the evidence was that there were a few malefactors who committed misdemeanours or crimes of dishonesty or who took people to dig trenches from time to time, but it did not disclose that they were homicidal, it did not disclose that they were racially prejudiced, it did not disclose that they were bigoted, it did not disclose that they were thought to be any of those things. It did not disclose that Sefer Halilovic thought they were any of those things. And in fact the evidence about the choice of those troops was, first of all, that Sefer Halilovic did not choose the individual troops, and secondly that that choice as it happened was quite a reasonable choice. You must not allow hindsight to pollute the picture that people at the time making their decisions had. It cannot be permitted to say that because some of these men may have and two of them did commit crimes, that such a fact must have been obvious at the time. It wasn't obvious to any of the players at the time. And the Prosecution did not prove that it was obvious or should have been obvious to Mr. Halilovic, nor that he had the relevant information in his hand at the time. The Prosecution had to prove, as they undertook in the indictment, that Sefer Halilovic actually knew there were killings going on. We say the Prosecution did not prove that Sefer Halilovic went to Grabovica on the 8th of September, that he heard the comment made by Vehbija Karic. We say the Prosecutor didn't prove that such a comment was made by Vehbija Karic. They called evidence that was unworthy of this Tribunal in their attempt and we don't blame the Prosecutor for trying, this is a serious matter and they are entitled to try but they failed. And they did not prove that Sefer Halilovic was told of these crimes while they were going on. And now we need to turn to the indictment itself. Your Honours, I'm not sure if the -- if Your Honours have in court copies of the indictment. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move to strike that last comment, please. It's uncalled for. Humorous but uncalled for, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the last comment is relevant in the mainstream of the opening statement so it's -- suspect not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution case, as pleaded, asserted a number of facts. Would Your Honours open the indictment, please, at paragraph 5. And I'll -- Your Honours, I'll take you through the allegations that are made and how they were structured. Your Honours will see that at paragraph 5 of the indictment, it was said that Sefer Halilovic had visited Grabovica on at least two occasions, and the Prosecution did prove that Halilovic went to Grabovica on the left bank on the 1st of September and they did prove that he passed through it in a car with Sefko Hodzic on or about the 3rd of September. Paragraph 6, the Prosecution asserted that these units had notorious reputations for being criminal and uncontrolled in behaviour. Your Honours, that raises a real problem with the pleadings here. If you go back to paragraph number 4, you'll see an averment that Sefer Halilovic was the commander of the operation and as such the troops involved in the Neretva 93 Operation were under his command and control.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: These include the 9th Motorised Brigade, the 10th Mountain Brigade, the 2nd Independent Battalion and the Prozor Independent Battalion. Now we have to point out that never was the 9th Motorised Brigade or the 10th Mountain Brigade said by any witness to be under the command of Sefer Halilovic. The order of the 2nd of September 1993, the number of which is Exhibit 161, made quite clear that troops from those units -- sorry, that the commander of the 1st Corps Vahid Karavelic, was to assemble a group of soldiers selected from a range of units specified in that order, and never was the 9th Brigade subordinated, the 9th Motorised Brigade subordinated to any operation at all. The reason I raise that in this context is that the Prosecution persistently failed to distinguish between the 9th Brigade as a body and the troops who were selected to go to Herzegovina. There was no evidence that the troops who went to Herzegovina had a bad reputation or a criminal past. There was never a suggestion that these troops were bad or had committed any offences. Of course, the Defence says that even the worst gossip and third-hand information which was tendered by the Prosecutors only ever established that some people in the 9th Brigade committed some misdemeanours and took people to dig trenches. And never did they establish that there was a homicidal or racially prejudiced tendency in that unit. But they simply didn't come to grips with the issue of the troops themselves who went, who left. And now, Your Honours, it's too late. Your Honours, at paragraph 8, the Prosecution averred that a unit of the 9th Motorised Brigade which was under the command of the deputy Brigade commander Ramiz Delalic left Sarajevo on the 7th of September. The date is not in dispute but the Prosecution did not prove that unit was under the command of Ramiz Delalic. Indeed in one of the most astounding performances that you can imagine they called Ramiz Delalic to say the contrary. They called him here declining to say in advance which parts of his evidence were truthful and which weren't and led that evidence from him. So to press on, Your Honours, at paragraph 10, the Prosecution put some allegations. We say, and I've already said this, that they did not prove the contends of this paragraph. They did not prove the comment by Karic, they did not prove the presence of Halilovic. But what's very important is that in the indictment, as it stands now, and up to paragraph 10, there is no allegation at that point of any criminal failure by Halilovic. That allegation arises only when you get to paragraph 15. And there, in paragraph 15, the Prosecution's case is to be found, that Halilovic was notified, that's actual notice, he was notified during the night of the 8th of September 1993 about the killing of civilians. Once he was notified and having knowledge of the criminal reputation of the 9th Motorised and 10th Mountain Brigades and having been present earlier in the day when Vehbija Karic made the remark referred to in paragraph 10 above, Sefer Halilovic was duty bound to act urgently and it's at that point that the Prosecution pleaded the duty that arose. We'll go on in a minute to see what steps he should have taken but it was central to the Prosecution case that Halilovic was in fact notified. That's what they say. They must be held to it. Your Honours, that case that Halilovic was notified during the night of the 8th of September 1993 collapsed in the running here and it's to be seen in the future whether the Prosecution persists with it. But Your Honours may have benefited from a proofing chart that the Prosecution provided. The Prosecution pursuant to a request by the Court and quite properly provided a guide entitled proofing chart to what evidence they led to prove parts of the indictment. And with respect to the question of whether Sefer Halilovic heard about the crimes while they were happening, the sole piece of evidence pointed to is a passage from the statement of Halilovic to the OTP dated the 6th of May 1996, a document which has yet to be admitted into the evidence. But which in any event says no more than this, that Halilovic said he wanted to go there but was advised by Namik Dzankovic that there was still shooting in the sector. And that's the Prosecution quote. "Still shooting in the sector." And that is said to constitute evidence of knowledge of the crimes while they were being committed. And that's all. Now, that evidence could not even if it was admitted from the bar table, and in the form it currently is, could not constitute proof that the crimes were ongoing at that point. Dzankovic doesn't say that in his evidence, and his evidence was unchallenged here by Prosecution or Defence. The terms of the phrase attributed to Halilovic there, if you admit this into evidence, which you have not done at this point, say no more than that there was the sound of shooting in the area. Your Honours have heard overwhelming evidence that from an early time when these troops arrived, there was shooting, some of it festive and fun-loving, some of it no doubt lethal and terrifying. But this evidence does not prove that one person pleaded as a murdered victim on the indictment, was alive at that moment. The case of actual notice in my submission is finished. The Prosecution went on to say that it was upon the receipt of that notice that Halilovic was duty bound to act urgently. He had duties and the Prosecution then sets them out to take steps, to eliminate a further threat and danger to surviving civilians, by evacuating them or ensuring they were properly protected. Then the Prosecution goes on to list how that could be done. It says, to accomplish this Sefer Halilovic should have given orders, done the things that are set out. All of those measures pleaded arise and are pleaded to arise once he knows, once he knew. They had to prove that he knew. So, Your Honours, that's why we say we think there is another case coming. Now, the Prosecution later in its second pre-trial brief sought to suggest that there were duties that arose the previous afternoon, the afternoon of the 8th. And in that pre-trial brief, you can see that it was said that Halilovic had duties once he heard the comment of Karic. Your Honours, we say that's outside of the indictment as it's pleaded. The indictment was a notice indictment, an actual notice indictment. But there are all sorts of problems with the alternative case that the Prosecution might seek to advance. We say of course that the chief Defence to all of this is to say well that incident on the 8th of September did not happen and in any event Halilovic was not there in the village. But the Prosecutor did not prove that that comment was to be taken seriously or was taken seriously and indeed all of those details are missing because the evidence came only from one person, Witness D. Now, we say therefore as a matter of form and as a matter of substance that the Prosecution's alternative approach to that crime ought to be rejected. They shouldn't go outside the indictment. But equally they shouldn't -- if they were permitted to rely upon that evidence we say it is not proved. And if the Prosecution are deprived of the actual notice on the night of the 8th, if they are deprived of the presence of Halilovic at Grabovica and his witnessing the comment by Karic, then all that remains is the choice of the troops, and that was never pleaded as a basis of liability for this crime, and nor could it be on its own a basis for liability for this crime, bearing in mind what you know. The Defence does not concede that the selection of troops could ever on its own in any circumstances constitute enough, but you don't have to decide that point and the battle won't be fought on that point, because it's comfortable to decide that issue on the facts of this case to say that these troops, the ones selected in the presence of Vahid Karavelic to go to Herzegovina were not known to be bad, were not thought to be bad, were not considered appropriate -- inappropriate, I'm sorry, and shouldn't have been seen in that light. And indeed the failure of the Prosecution to prove any details of the crime scene at all with the exception of the -- what the dense says is dishonest evidence by Witness D and Muhanic and honest but partial evidence of -- sorry, just excuse me. Sorry, the partial but we say honest and accurate evidence of Mr. Sakrak. The Prosecution did not show who the killers were. They did not show that most of these people were murdered, and they just provided a real paucity of material concerning that. So the Defence said that the Prosecution did not prove their case in respect of that crime. When you look to the pre-trial brief by which I mean the second pre-trial brief the amended one which replaced the first, it will be apparent that at paragraphs 95, 97 and 98, the Prosecution seek to place more emphasis on the Grabovica incident but applying the proper standard of proof to that, we say it's finished. It's almost unimaginable, and we ask you to consider this, that Sefer Halilovic would stand by and let it happen, knowing what you know about him. It was completely in his interest to stop it. He had to stop it. The Defence did not prove that this ruined his life, but we don't have to. It's obvious that this event, and both events, were utter disasters for him. You can gain -- sorry, I withdraw that. Very well. I turn now to the next mode of guilt that is alleged against Sefer Halilovic, and that is the failure to punish the crime at Grabovica. Now, Your Honours -- pardon me a moment, please. We want to point out that in dealing with this crime, you are dealing with a crime which generally speaking would be seen as a lesser level of magnitude than the failure to prevent. The moral culpability of a failure to prevent would generally, though not as a mathematical question, be worse than a failure to punish afterwards. But in the case of Halilovic now, and in the case of Grabovica, the Prosecution, leaving aside the allegations raised by Ramiz Delalic in this Court, the Prosecution case is one that he was imperfect. I'll come to the details of that in a minute but I just want to read something from the High Command case. "Modern war such as the last war entails a large measure of decentralisation. A high commander cannot keep completely informed of the details of military operations of subordinates and most assuredly not of every administrative measure. He has the right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed. The president of the United States is commander of its m military forces. Criminal acts committed by those forces cannot themselves be charged to him on the theory of subordination. The same is true of other high commanders in the chain of command. Criminality does not attach to every individual in this chain of command from that fact alone. There must be personal dereliction." Now the gravity of that dereliction can be measured by the consequences for Sefer Halilovic. According to the law, it makes a murderer of him. So the question then becomes: Did the Prosecution prove such a dereliction on behalf of Sefer Halilovic? The big picture again -- perhaps what I'll do is present the big picture view from the Defence perspective and then say something about the specifics that could have been -- that you would expect. The big picture here is that Sefer Halilovic found out about this crime on the 9th of September. If you find that the troops were under his effective control, if you find that, and we say that you shouldn't, then on any view, that ceased on the 19th of September when they went back to Sarajevo. The relevant period in which to assess Halilovic's culpability for this crime is between the 9th and the 19th of September. That's how it's pleaded in the indictment and that's how common sense and how the evidence says it should have been dealt with, too. Because if troops were the 9th Brigade were sent back to Herzegovina at a later time, nobody says they were the same troops and there is no suggestion to that effect. So you are looking at a ten-day period. You are not looking at a person who closed his eyes to repeated abuses. You are not dealing with someone who allowed a reign of terror to unfold. You're dealing with one incident concerning troops who were, even if the Prosecution proves its case of effective control, who ceased to be in effective control after that time. Now, what the Defence says in the big picture of this case is that Sefer Halilovic launched an investigation, and he did so through the appropriate organ. He launched an investigation and he chose the right people to do the job. Now the right people to do the job were the SVB, the military security service. One of whose reasons to exist is to perform the work of the police in a military setting, as we shall demonstrate by very simple analysis of the relevant rules which have been tendered into evidence here for that exact purpose and which you, as professional judges, will easily comprehend. By taking the step that he did, Sefer Halilovic started the ball rolling, started the investigation, and took the investigation out of his control, and you know that because the SVB had its own separate structure, its own line of reporting, its own obligations. The evidence discloses that the SVB, the military security service, did investigate the crime and that they kept investigating the crime after Sefer Halilovic's connection with these troops. Whatever you find that to be, was severed on the 19th of September. We say the Prosecution here found themselves in a difficult position because, as will become apparent in a moment, they pleaded the wrong rules. And as was frankly conceded by the Prosecutor, they just don't know what the rules were that Sefer Halilovic should have followed. They don't know what the law is, they don't know it now, they didn't know it then. How can Halilovic be expected to know it? We don't criticise the Prosecutor. The fact is they looked. They found nothing. You cannot assume that the Prosecutor simply dropped the ball. They didn't plead it because they can't. Now, Your Honours, we say the SVB were the appropriate authority to do the job. First of all, Sefer Halilovic was a senior military officer in the field. He had a job, and every one agrees that he had the job of coordinating combat activities in that area on a very wide front. The Prosecution of course go further and say that he wasn't merely coordinating but that he was effectively commanding and indeed they plead that he was the de jure commander as well. But whether he was the commander or not or merely a coordinator, there was a war on. There was active combat activity starting on the 13th of September and occurring every single day of the 10 days that Sefer Halilovic had thereafter. I'll show you why you can be sure of that in a moment. But the SVB were able to investigate. The SVB can coordinate across areas. They are not regionalised. Although the SVB officers are attached to their local brigade, the SVB through its line of -- its own professional line of reporting, can simultaneously investigate in more than one place. It was quite appropriate and it was inevitable that Sefer Halilovic would have to delegate this task to someone. He had to. He's not a policeman. Senior military officer is entitled to delegate and that's what he did. Did he delegate correctly? We say yes. When you look at what happened, Namik Dzankovic was properly tasked by Sefer Halilovic to investigate. Dzankovic did launch an investigation. Dzankovic, when he was launched into this investigation, the whole SVB was launched with him because he reports to them separately. And so it is that you find other SVB directors and commanders in the area taking an interest and contributing to the investigation, so Nermin Eminovic contributed to it, joined it. Zajko Sahirlic joined it. At the end of this case, we'll endeavour to put some sense into the string of orders. It's just not feasible to do it now in the time that we have. But it's obvious that the SVB this, not just Namik Dzankovic but the institution, joined in the investigation. And in the end, and not too far in the future, six to seven weeks into the future perhaps. Five weeks perhaps into the future, the Grabovica investigation became one of the bases for questioning the men arrested during the Trebevic Operation on 26th of October. Now, the Prosecutors in effective and well measured opening in this case said that all Mr. Halilovic did was to commission a report. But that was an inaccurate statement and was not proved by the evidence. He started an investigation, the investigation happened. Now, not only did he start the investigation, but his superiors were notified. The last witness to give evidence was Bakir Alispahic and he said that when he got back to Sarajevo, Rasim Delic, the commander of the army, knew about it. Alispahic himself approached the president, Alija Izetbegovic, as he had to do, as he was bound to do, as everyone knew he must do. Jusuf Jasarevic, the chief of the military security service, knew about it. Now, we say that Namik Dzankovic acted sensibly. Exhibit P214 was a document that is a report of Namik Dzankovic and it was dated the 13th of September. And in that document, Namik Dzankovic proposed certain measures. It's on the final page of that document. It's okay, Your Honours. I don't have my copy in front of me now about I don't need it. I have to say I'm able to -- but Your Honours will find it on the last page of the English section. And Your Honours, there, Mr. Dzankovic made proposals that were thorough, sensible, and professional. We say it was an appropriate and measured response to the real situation in which he found himself. Your Honours, I'm told I gave the wrong number. I apologise for that. It's 215. Your Honours, I -- it can be brought up on the screen but I don't mean Your Honours to have to read it for the 15th time here. I'll simply point to the measures that Dzankovic suggested should happen. He noted that Halilovic had distanced himself from it, from the crime, and he noticed that Halilovic ordered him personally to work together with other military security service member and MUP officials - I'll come to the MUP officials in a minute - to collect as much information as possible about the infamous event. "Pursuant to the above I propose the following," and then he listed all of the things that could be done including crime scene investigations, including the getting of doctors, experts, and, generally speaking, what you see from Namik Dzankovic there is a sensible response. There was some queries leveled at Namik Dzankovic's level of professionalism, not, I hasten to say, while he was here, Your Honours. But the fact remains that the criticisms leveled at Dzankovic might be seen as self-serving criticisms but in any event, do not impact on Sefer Halilovic. We say you'd find that Dzankovic, whatever he lacked in experience, did the best he could in a difficult situation, but if you make a finding that he made some mistakes, we don't agree that he did, but if you make that finding, no one suggests that Halilovic knew or should have known that he did. Sefer Halilovic didn't choose this man, didn't know him. He was chosen by Jusuf Jasarevic because he was on the terrain already. He was not presented to Sefer Halilovic as a lame duck. And we say Sefer Halilovic was entitled to rely upon the competence and good faith of Namik Dzankovic. And we go further and say that that was entirely justified and Dzankovic did what could be done in the situation that existed at that time. Now, to proceed with that, with that argument a little bit further, you have to see Halilovic's actions in the context of the time. He was coordinating, and as I say the Prosecution go further even and say that he had the more onerous task of commanding, a ragtag army in the process of being brought under the line of command and control which had unprofessional officers doing the best they could and soldiers who were doing the best they could in a very difficult situation. He was short of weapons, communication equipment, petrol, and in short he had a very trying and busy job to do at that time. He had to delegate, and the job that he was doing is not one that he could lightly put aside. The evidence as to the situation in Mostar is overwhelmingly bad. The situation in Mostar was a humanitarian disaster. You would be entitled to act on that without any thought -- well, not without any thought. With thought, but without any hesitation. So then we come to the issue of the Prosecution's suggestion as to how Halilovic should have responded. In the indictment, at paragraph 36, you will see that the Prosecutor averred the ABiH disciplinary regulations, in particular those gazetted on the 13th of August 1992, as amended to implement the rules relating to the investigation of war crimes also bound him. Now, Your Honour, my learned friend tendered the disciplinary rules in the course of his case. It was Exhibit 103. And relying on that document represented a fundamental misunderstanding of what options there were open to a commander. You don't use these disciplinary rules to investigate major crimes. These rules concerned disciplinary infractions and, as Article 1 says, "these rules shall regulate military discipline, disciplinary measures and disciplinary punishment for breeches of military discipline." The punishment set out there in -- are relatively minor ones. It's not the appropriate body of law to apply. The Prosecution, when it turned to deal with this matter in the proofing chart provided to the Court -- will Your Honours just excuse me, it's a lengthy document. Referred to a number of the other documents that were tendered. But the military discipline rules did not form a part of what should have been Halilovic's resources. Creates a very interesting question, one which we don't have to resolve for this Tribunal as to what contribution domestic law can make but Halilovic dealt with an army which initially had no way of investigating crimes and the rule on the SVB was brought in, the rule on the military security service was brought in to adapt the Yugoslavian national army, the JNA's approach to dealing with that problem. Now, these documents -- sorry, this source of rules created the SVB and we'll go to some of the provisions of that in a minute. However, it's important that it be realised why it was that Halilovic was entitled to delegate, because he's not a professional, because he created a professional body that had exactly that competence. In looking at the SVB and its rules what you should look at is that those rules enable, they enable investigations to take place. This is not a question of a commander hiding behind a body of law and saying that he meritlessly complied with some of the steps. It's not that case. Instead, Halilovic brought into being - of course, with the Presidency, he's not a legislator of his own - the rules on the SVB -- just excuse me one moment, please. So D -- sorry, not D; exhibit 137 is the rules for the military security service in the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in the past ages which have been read out before in this court, the competence of this organisation is spelled out. And that's at section 39, 40, and 41. At 39, under the heading "The Military Security Service in Criminal Proceedings," that "the rules provide that the work and powers of the internal affairs organs, as laid down by the ZKP relate also to the conduct of an action taken by authorised officers of the military security service, in pre-trial and criminal proceedings" - the distinction there is not without significance - "within the frame of their competence." Now, you will remember there that some of the terms were explained in court, ZKP refers to the Criminal Code, the civil code that was in place, and the pre-trial and criminal proceedings, one referred -- pre-trial refers to what we might call the investigative phase, sometimes in this court it was called the pre-criminal phase but the time before a criminal denunciation is laid with the military Prosecutor, and criminal proceedings which is from the commencement of proceedings themselves. There is an extended version of what a trial is. It's different to the common law system and different from some civil systems as well. So what that provides, that section, is that the military security service has the powers that the MUP civilian police have in their area of competence when dealing with offences that are within the competence of the SVB. So paragraph 40 then goes on to provide some specifics. When there is reasonable suspicion that a criminal offence triable by military courts has been committed officers of the military security service must take the necessary measures. I just note the imperative phraseology, must take the necessary measures to find the perpetrator of the criminal offence, to prevent the perpetrator or his accomplice going into hiding or escaping, to uncover, protect the evidence and exhibits which can serve as evidence. Together, all the information useful for successful conduct of the criminal proceedings. And then, once that's done at paragraph 41, on the basis of the information gathered, officers of the military security service in the command of the brigade or corresponding or a higher ranking officers in the military security service shall submit a criminal report to the competent military Prosecutor's office. Now, the SVB were fully competent to perform the investigative task. You will see that they have various rights. One right that may be worth noticing is at paragraph 7(E) where it is made clear that within the range - this is at page 6 of the B/C/S copy, Your Honours - "within the range of military police assignments, the military security service shall perform the following tasks," and then down at point E, professionally direct the work of the authorised members of military police in pre-trial proceedings. It was quite right of Sefer Halilovic to delegate the investigation to the SVB. Now, can Sefer Halilovic's choices at that time be criticised at all? The Defence says no. The Defence says he made the right choice. In the context he had, he had a military operation to conduct. The failure to conduct that military operation had serious human rights implications for the people living in Mostar. There were all sorts of reasons why he had to go on with that operation. On the Prosecution's own case, he had an order to command that operation. And never was he told to stop it. The Prosecution have to do more than to point out imperfections. It's not open now for them to plead different imperfections. But should the Prosecution seek to design some councils of perfection for Mr. Halilovic they are doomed to fail because, and I'm not going to speculate as to what they might be. But it was not appropriate to stop the action. It was not appropriate to barge into Grabovica and start a war. Your Honours have heard already precisely what the situation was when arrests had been attempted with members of the 9th Brigade, 10th Brigade in the past. And there is another thing. In this case, the investigation was clearly and openly obstructed by the Prosecution witness Ramiz Delalic. He said it wasn't. He said that Sefer Halilovic just fresh from planning the murder of his own commander, proposed and executed a cover-up of this crime. But the evidence from independent witnesses was crushing on that score. As early as 3.00 in the afternoon on the 9th of September, Ramiz Delalic expressed hostility to the investigation and indifference to the plight of the Croats on the bridge when he was met by one of the two individuals, Salihamidzic and Kurt who went to the village. The following evening on the 10th, in front of several witnesses, none of whom were challenged in this Court, and whose evidence ought to be simply accepted without any difficulty, he showed again an indifference to the crimes, a hostility to the police, and an intention to leave the zone of combat. Now, this is a man who the Prosecution wish to say was under the control and command of Sefer Halilovic and whose units they say were under his command and control. And Your Honours might pause to reflect on that if you need to be subtle about it. But I don't think there is any need for subtlety here; it's quite clear Delalic blocked the investigation. The Defence does not say that you ought to find Ramiz Delalic killed people. We don't say that. You might find that he was upset to hear of the crimes, and you might not. There is evidence of a competing nature with respect to his response. Because on the one hand, it may be accepted that he demonstrated anger in hearing about the crime. On the other hand, it's quite clear that he kept the children overnight in the village from the 9th until the 10th. That's just clearly proved and not explained by him, and of course it's inconsistent with his very spiteful allegations made about Halilovic wanting to have those children put away. It's inconsistent with that, but it's also rather significant about what he was doing. You might take the view that those children were bargaining chips in the hands of Ramiz Delalic. But that riddle is a riddle only because you can't believe Ramiz, and the children of course don't know what Delalic had in mind himself. They can just say what he did. Of course, that was done honesty and believably in this Court. However you read that riddle, in the end the answer is simple: That Halilovic had a disaster on his hands with that man, Ramiz Delalic. And it means that it just wasn't viable, even if there were troops available, even if military victory was assurable, even if there were no other matters to deal with, it wasn't viable to just barge in and arrest people. And it's always been in any event one of the Prosecutor's, we say, gaps of -- of argument. It's not a lack of intellect by any means, it's just a gap in their argument that there were no suspects. You don't just barge into a village and arrest anyone. The troops would be entitled to fight back in that circumstance. There were no suspects identified. The Prosecution didn't point to any. Didn't try. That's the failure -- when the Prosecution point to that failure, you have to bear that in mind, that Halilovic had many jobs to do. He was on the terrain, he was backwards and forwards, and he was entitled to rely upon those he delegated it to. We say that you wouldn't find fault with that, but if the Prosecution do identify fault, then it's not something that renders Halilovic a murderer. It's not such a gross dereliction that you would trouble to convict him of murder. Your Honours, could we take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's time for us to take a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, before you continue, do you have any matters to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do. The Court was kind enough to allow us to have until today to prepare this opening and I -- I indicated that I was relatively -- feeling relatively unwell last week. I'm -- I'm getting better now. I would prefer not to start the next witness if that suited the Court's convenience, otherwise we will complete the rest of the witnesses that we have for this week, for another reason I'll indicate. But I think I'll go long enough that we would only have maybe an hour to 40 minutes left for this witness tonight and frankly, I'm -- for myself, I would seek the indulgence that we not start him until tomorrow. I think we'll finish him tomorrow. I can't speak for the Prosecutor, but I suspect we will. His evidence is pretty confined. There was a witness scheduled here, I think we sent a note concerning this matter, but one of the witnesses has been withdrawn. The witness -- so he won't be coming. The witness that -- I'm just not naming names because I'm not sure whether I'm going to make any applications in the future, but there was one witness that I indicated that had a -- a health issue that's to be resolved tomorrow afternoon. As we understand it, he's -- we hope he'll be okay and he'll come and he's a witness that will probably take two days. The other witness that I indicated I was giving consideration to or giving consideration to and we are proposing not to call that witness. So we now are reduced to two witnesses for this week. We will comfortably finish those. Your Honour, could I just indicate too that I'm aware of having -- that in some respects the Defence is -- seems to be going at an uneven pace in terms of calling these -- the witnesses. We think the time we take is shortening matters. We are going to call -- we have indicated a confined case. It's very much on the cards that I will cut another witness as well. I'll keep the Prosecution advised of that as soon as I make a decision. That's -- but we are not going to go longer. We are going to go shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. But don't forget the 92 bis witnesses, because the Prosecution is waiting for the statements of those witnesses and they have to give us a reply on whether they want to cross-examine those witnesses or not or whether they did not agree with your proposal. And could I ask you how long do you think your direct examination will take for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I thought about 90 minutes. It could go a tiny bit more but it's as indicated in the notes. The only reason I think it would go anything over one hour because I want to show him a couple of documents, as indicated, and he's also drawn two diagrams which -- I think they have been -- I hope they have been provided to the Prosecutor. They are just his drawings actually, but the Defence wants to offer those just to explain what the strategic situation was facing his unit which was right next door to the Uzdol -- to the Prozor Independent Battalion so that the Tribunal can see what was envisaged to be achieved and that may assist, certainly will assist as background and it may assist in some specific matters as well. There are two such diagrams that he's drawn but the diagrams should shorten things so, yes, 90 minutes, I think, is what I'm budgeting for, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, is it possible for you to start the witness today? And we may have an early break tomorrow when we finish that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, it's entirely possible and that's what we will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll continue with the next witness today, maybe for an hour or 45 minutes and tomorrow morning we will continue and then we'll break whenever we finish that witness. Is that agreeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fine with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Well, let's continue your opening statement, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I've really come to the end of the failure to what I want to say in this -- these opening remarks about the failure to punish at Grabovica and I would make this comment about -- about that failure to punish. Without the evidence -- Ramiz Delalic gave evidence here and his evidence was not really evidence of a failure to punish. It was evidence of a criminal conspiracy by Sefer Halilovic and Zulfikar Alispago and what was said by him was that those two planned to cover up the crime and as an incident of that crime were proposing at one point at least to do away with the two children, the two young boys. Now, for reasons that we will go into later on, for reasons that we hope we submit are obvious, we ask the Tribunal to reject that evidence as being self-serving evidence, that we say that Ramiz Delalic had to tell the story of Halilovic covering up because he covered up because he committed offences because he owed his position to his men and he couldn't see his men investigated and whatever his reasons may be, there are all sorts of possible reasons, and but whatever they are, that's why he makes the allegation. He's got a good motive to lie and it's to save his own skin. If you set aside, as you should, the evidence of Ramiz Delalic, then what you're left with really is a very reasonable, the Defence says, conduct from Halilovic. It may be possible for the ingenuity of Prosecutors after the event to device strategies. The witnesses did not give any comfort in that regard. And this Tribunal would not visit upon Mr. Halilovic a verdict of guilt of murder because he didn't achieve perfection. Now, before I turn to the failure to punish the killings at Uzdol, I want to make a couple of general remarks partly because the inferences to be drawn are -- because -- partly because we are coming to an inference part of the case, a conclusions-from-other-conclusions part of the case. I made some comments early on about the standard of proof that must be met in terms of important facts and I said, and the Tribunal knows better than I do, of course, that those important facts have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, each one. And in this case, there are a number of inferences that the Prosecution seeks to have you draw, conclusions based on other facts. They don't lead direct evidence but they seek to rely upon inferences and, frankly, the Defence also points to inferences. There is no fault from the Prosecution's position in doing that, and indeed experience shows that a circumstantial case can be the -- the most important of all. It doesn't rely on human frailty to the same degree. So -- or test human frailty to the same degree. But when dealing with an inferential case, when you are reasoning as Judges faced with a number of facts and you're confronted with a request by the Prosecutor to draw a further fact as an inference from those facts, then it's important amidst the welter and the weight of many facts to bear in mind what you know but you have to remind yourselves of it at all times, and that is to ensure that inferences in a criminal case are proved to the criminal standard. Important inferences have got to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Inferences which are facts proved by inference, which are important in the Prosecution case have to be proved beyond reasonable doubt. Now, in assessing inferences, you are always entitled to look at all the facts and your experience as professional judges is -- is very important and it means that you don't have to be given the warnings that juries in the common law system are given, they have to be given lengthy instructions about that reasoning process. You don't have to -- have to be given those, but it's important to bear in mind a couple of, if you like, extra factors when drawing inferences. First is that the Prosecution have got to show that the inference they seek is the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. And in that regard, the Prosecution in this case have assumed a much heavier burden than usual, and you know that because you know that this Prosecution is particularly adversarial, that they have been prepared to deny you evidence which they were going to rely upon and which they mean to call until it proved inconvenient. You saw, for example, the tendering of a document signed by an individual named Mujezinovic. That was a document commenting upon Sefer Halilovic's media exploits. Well, they wanted to rely on that document but they were drew from Mr. Mujezinovic. That has a direct affect on the weight you could give that document, of course, and you don't need to have that explained now. But it does rather reveal this Prosecutor's strategy. When Bahrudin Comor came along and gave the wrong answers, they were drew him. Now, Your Honours, this system is adversarial. The Prosecutors are not here to do favours for the Defence nor should they be. But in the civil systems, Prosecutors have a higher duty and are trusted, and here at the Tribunal, when the Prosecutor takes the adversarial position which they took, then when you assess whether an inference ought to be drawn from a selection of facts put forward by the Prosecutor, you have to think to yourself, well, I'm not being dealt a fair deck of cards here. I'm not being given a full picture by the Prosecutor. Now, the Prosecutors and the Defence are in an absolutely different position. The Prosecutor has to meet the burden of proof and they have to prove it to a high standard. The Defence's job is to point to doubts about that. The Defence does not have a burden to prove innocence, nor can it. It's a function of the adversarial system. It's a function of the standard of proof that we -- that the Prosecution has to meet, and one pragmatic thing that might lie behind it is just the resources. The Defence just can't go proving innocence in the face of the might of the Prosecution. We don't complain. The Prosecution should have huge resources because they've got a huge job to do across the country. But as it plays out in this case here, it's for the Prosecutor to put the facts forward and they cannot do that in this case saying to you that they have assisted the Tribunal to find the truth. They are adversaries in this case and have conducted themselves as adversaries throughout. And this is not meant to be a complaint about that. They will conduct themselves as they see fit. Nor are they on trial. I'm defending Sefer Halilovic. But when you come to consider the inferences they invite you to draw, you know you're being given what they choose to give, not what they have to give. And the Prosecution made a decision not to call its investigator in this case. The evidence from Ramiz Delalic was extremely worrying about that. Delalic plainly assisted procuring the witnesses who they did call and plainly was closely associated with the impugned investigator, and that is a further matter that you can take into account when invited to draw an inference. You don't criticise the Prosecution's morals or ethics. We are not asking that to be done. What we are saying is you're being given half a story and because of that you may expose the inferences they seek to very close scrutiny indeed. That really introduces the Prosecution case in relation to Uzdol. This was a hollow case. They led very little evidence. The Prosecution led the barest minimum, not enough, we say, to found a conviction. Not enough for you to have any sense of satisfaction as to what happened at Uzdol. Not enough to allow you to have any sense of who had the duty, if there was a duty, to investigate what happened there. Not enough to draw any conclusion as to whether or not there was an investigation there. Now, the Prosecution took a decision to call no evidence on the question of whether or not an investigation happened. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: (redacted) Elicit the answer after 11 years, no, and rest. Now, that's not good enough. This is a war crime that's being charged here. We say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, closed session, please. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful to the Prosecutor for indicating that and I think I should indicate that at all times I'm open to being corrected on that matter, as I have been on a number of other occasions. Well, Your Honours, that was the Prosecution's position in respect of Uzdol, that they did not call any evidence that could answer the question whether or not there was an investigation. Of course, the Defence was in a position to put certain documents to the witnesses who were called to indicate that there was an investigation that inquiries were made and that reports were sought and reports were given. And that conclusions were drawn about what happened in Uzdol. So the Defence says in respect of that, the Prosecution did not prove that Halilovic had effective control of those troops. We say the Prosecution did not prove that Halilovic had a duty to investigate or to punish this matter. We say that the Prosecution did not prove that there was any failure to investigate. And finally, depending upon the finding of fact made by the Tribunal, if you were tempted, if you were not tempted, if you did find against what we say is the weight of the evidence, that there was a failure by Sefer Halilovic to investigate, that that failure had nothing to do with the failure to bring any particular people to justice, and that it is too minimal and too remote to be a war crime and to be the war crime of murder. To say that Sefer Halilovic committed murder over an unspecified failure at Uzdol is stretching that term beyond what it's about. It really does raise the issue generally speaking, Your Honour, of -- of what this Tribunal seeks to achieve. It doesn't seek to stretch the law to accommodate Sefer Halilovic. It wasn't put here for Sefer Halilovic or for his sort of conduct and that's why we ask for a very mainstream approach which we know and we do expect. Now, as to Uzdol, the village and what happened there, the Prosecution's failures to we say the Prosecution committed failure after failure in relation to that and we are going to point to them in detail at the end of the case. But the big picture, if you like, and I've tried to do this in respect to each one. The big picture with respect to Uzdol is this it was an armed outpost where really civilian life had ceased to happen in any meaningful way. The school was occupied by the -- the school had ceased functioning. The civilians generally speaking had been moved to Prozor and they had been accommodated in houses which in some mysterious way had become empty in Prozor and what happened, Your Honour, was that the shop was closed, the houses were occupied generally by soldiers, such civilians as remained were people who came back and were generally speaking involved in supporting the combat troops in their combat tasks, cooking, doing home guard, so on. The pity of it was is that people -- certain people for whatever reason, which they would themselves, I have no doubt, regret, had brought some small children back with them. This is a village where civilians generally speaking had weapons or access to weapons, where the evidence was absolutely clear that civilians did have guns in their house. And where the evidence is clear that there was a battle. Now, we ask you to set aside the evidence of the witness Kate Adie who came and gave evidence. Perhaps it could be said she gave her evidence in good faith but she just didn't have the expertise or the time to do what she says she did, and unfortunately, the Defence lass to make some criticisms of what she did even as a journalist. She just didn't ask questions. But you would not have any hesitation to dismiss her claims that there was a systematic house-to-house hunt because the evidence just doesn't support that. What we have in this Court was clear evidence that there was an exchange of fire in the villages. You remember Mr. Stojanovic. It was the person who ran down the road and jumped over his mother who he thought was dead. It turned out she wasn't, and luckily she wasn't. He agrees that he had an exchange of fire or at least fired shots towards the attackers. You saw the videotape, you might recall, of the elderly gentleman who was a survivor who lived and he was showing the cameraman where his gun was. You might also recall on that occasion how the sound went mysteriously blank at that point on the tape. It's just one of those mysteries of nature that has never been exchanged in this case. But anyway, we did restore that and we were able to play it and it turns out he did have a gun. You had the book concerning Uzdol where the mother of the three poor children, Mrs. Zelic, was praised for throwing hand grenades at the incoming troops. And you had other witnesses giving evidence about hand grenades. And in short, although you can't say that each person did or did not have a weapon, and the evidence just doesn't tell you that, you can't infer that the attackers here, the people who came in, thought they were dealing with civilians. Now, what happened in the -- what happened in the villages of Uzdol is not explained. You may have had people kicking in doors and shooting whoever was inside. There could be all sorts of explanations. You could have that sort of thing happening leaving close-up injuries. The failure to prove the crime base is really important in that case because the Prosecution, as one of the elements and one of the many elements have got to prove that these were murders and are murders of people who were not taking part in combat hostilities, and also that the killers didn't think they were taking part in combat activities. The Prosecution just didn't try in respect of that. Now, there are a small number of killed and that's -- and what I say when I -- what I mean by this is that the Prosecution have to prove their case. I do not mean to suggest in saying this that any victim, person killed, at Uzdol brought their fate on their head, deserved death or pain, but the Prosecution have the onus of proving it, according to law, that each was a murder, and unfortunately, there is no doubt, there can be no doubt, that this crime scene was played with. To what extent, you don't know. But you've got evidence of weapons, you've got evidence of civilian-clothed people shooting at the incoming soldiers, and by that I mean Mr. Stojanovic who you'll recall his own mother said was wearing a track suit when he was shooting. And with respect to each death, there really is a doubt, even the three children. That's not an area where the Defence has to fight the battle. None of that, no one says Halilovic had anything to do with that or knew about it, and it's far away from the guilt of Sefer Halilovic. But the Prosecution have got a prove it and they will have to specify to you how each one is proved. At the moment that -- there is just no sense that that's being done on the evidence. Your Honours, it really -- again, before I press on with that, raises another issue and that's the issue of, frankly, the victims here. The victims are not limited to the killed, the deceased in the case, although they are the only ones that are an element of the crime. The victims include the sad people left behind and the ones who would like to know what happened, and would like to know the answers. Now, it's part of the healing process of this Tribunal that everything comes out. That's the idea. And when the Prosecutor takes the adversarial stance that they did here and sculpt the evidence as they chose to do, and that's not what is happening in this Tribunal. No victim wants Sefer Halilovic. And explaining to victims how it was that Sefer Halilovic is there, and Ramiz Delalic and Witness D were there, is a challenging intellectual exercise. Now, the Prosecution did not prove that these troops were in the effective control of Sefer Halilovic. I was relatively brief about the way in which effective control should be dealt with in Grabovica because it's a long, tangled matter with many different parts of evidence. It's a little simpler with respect to Uzdol because in Uzdol you have a combat report by Enver Buza, the commander of the Prozor Independent Battalion who evidently did make an inquiry into what happened and reported on that. And he said in his report, which you have tendered into evidence, his combat report, that it was a combat activity that took place pursuant to an order, an order numbered 01/1500-27. Both Buza's combat report and the order that it relied on, order 1527 -- sorry, 1500-27 are in evidence in this case and Buza says that he was attacking Uzdol pursuant to an order of the 6th Corps Command. Now of course, the witness Salko Gusic said that Buza's unit was subordinated out of his command for that time, but that ought to be just disregarded and Mr. Gusic, you might regard as a witness who was running a mile from liability and to say he was not in the chain of command when in reality he was. And that order is just conclusive proof beyond any shadow of a doubt that that's the chain of command that existed at that time. Now, it's important to look without the benefit of hindsight and look at how people at the time dealt with the problem at Uzdol. Exhibit 227 was an inquiry from the head of the SVB, Jusuf Jasarevic, and when he heard about the Uzdol matter, he directed his inquiries not to Sefer Halilovic or to the inspection team but to the 6th Corps military security. Exhibit 159 was an exhibit where the deputy commander of the Bosnian army, standing in at that moment for Rasim Delic -- that deputy's name was Stjepan Siber and Siber sent a letter on the 16th of the 9th inquiring about what happened in Uzdol, and he sent that letter to the commander of the 6th Corps, not to Sefer Halilovic or to the inspection team. Exhibit 228, Jusuf Jasarevic, two days later on the 18th of the 9th again was directing his inquiries directly to the 6th Corps. Now, it's in that light that the Defence is going to call the witness (redacted). In one sense he's not necessary because we say that the evidence is very strong that at the time when news of Uzdol happened, the matter was dealt with in an appropriate way at the battalion level through the normal chain of command, from Siber, acting commander or deputy commander, through the 6th Corps command down to the battalion, Prozor Independent Battalion, back up again. Now, the Prosecution as we say embarked on the strategy of not leading any evidence about what happened. And in one respect it's unnecessary to call any evidence about it because the burden is on the Prosecutor, not on us, but because we found (redacted) we are going to call him. And he is -- he's a witness who was the (redacted). He'll say, Well, yes, I was asked and I did take statements and I drew a conclusion. And you can see later on in other material that's admitted into evidence what the conclusions were, that those who investigated, having taken statements, found that nothing had happened. Nothing illegal had happened, I should say. Plenty happened but nothing illegal happened. Now, again, it's important to put yourselves into the steps -- into the shoes of those who were actually faced with investigating. They had been chased out of the Uzdol village or villages and they had no opportunity to go there. In any event, you might form a view that there was some propaganda activities engaged in and it's a sad and amazing thing to see that you get a mixture of genuine grief and real sadness with the people who were killed and yet also at the same time a production. And that happened, and you can see what happened in the evidence of Kate Adie and others. But what could viably be done at that time was to take statements, to inquire among themselves. That's what could happen and that's what did happen.
